summary: After 2000, wave 1. The archive as object. A new Research-field entry archival_turn (period_4) gathers the readership that the History PhD citation graph identifies as the broadest post-2000 framework without an opposing side: the archive as a site of power (Trouillot, Mbembe, Schwartz and Cook), Stoler's reading along the grain and the Dutch reviewers' doubts, the archive's allure, fever and dust (Farge, Derrida, Steedman), absence and critical fabulation (Hartman, Fuentes), archive stories and the ethnography of archives (Burton, Dirks, Zeitlyn), and the archivists' turn in Canada and South Africa, in six strands, a roster of 16, a chronology of 27 events from 1989 to 2024, and seven field arrows (three more are held, include: false, after Sol's review). Ann Laura Stoler (promoted from a people record; 7 new edges, 15 events) and Michel-Rolph Trouillot (new; 8 edges, 24 events) become person entries in the historians layer. edge_386 and edge_417 are re-sourced from post to ann_laura_stoler; derrida_archive_primary loses its mirror-host URL. Settler colonial studies after 2000, and Patrick Wolfe (period-4 wave 1, Agent B). The entry settler_colonialism is reviewed through 2024: its description, scope note and figures are rewritten from texts read in full (Wolfe 2006, Veracini 2011 and 2016, Kauanui 2016, Englert 2020, Goeman 2016; Tuck and Yang 2012 and Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014 in most pages; Macoun and Strakosch 2013 in the authors' version); six strands are corrected and three added (the Wolfe–Veracini structure debate; Canadian history beside and under the frame, 2009–2020; the field's institutions); its chronology grows from 6 to 48 events (2008–2022) and its coverage to 2024; thirteen roster rows are amended and eleven added. Patrick Wolfe's entry is backfilled: description, scope note and figures from the 2006 essay read in full, a chronology of 24 events (1994–2022), six new incident edges (indigenous, racial formation, Holocaust historiography, postcolonial critique, Indigenous–newcomer relations, Harris's influence) and the field's critique of him; edge_892 and edge_893 are revised. Four entry-level edges are added (critique of Wolfe; dependency; Canadian working-class history; environmental history) and edge_881, edge_882 (now a critique of postcolonial studies) and edge_883 revised. Thirty-nine source records are added and seventeen amended; nine people records are added; Wolfe's Wikidata item (Q109284663) and five roster QIDs are checked by QLever SPARQL. Agent C, period-4 wave 1: environmental history after 2000. The environment entry gains a description and scope note to 2024, a dated chronology of twenty-one events from the merged journal (1996) to McNeill's AHA address (2020), four strands (the wilderness debate as a selected exchange; the Anthropocene and the climate of history; Canadian environmental history; conservation, dispossession and neighbouring historiographies), twenty roster rows (the Canadians, McNeill, Sutter, Jacoby, Spence, Foreman, Callicott, Nash, Isenberg, Malm, Bonneuil, Fressoz, Daschuk, Parr), three new edges (to indigenous, native_newcomer, capitalismdebates) and revisions of edge_112 and edge_720. William Cronon gains six edges (the wilderness critique received; contributions to indigenous, public and digital history; Leopold's influence; his reading of Worster), two edge revisions and twenty-two dated points to 2016. Donald Worster gains six edges (Merchant's and the field's critiques; contributions to the capitalism debates and the history of science; Leopold's and the Annales' influence), one edge revision and nineteen dated points to 2017. Forty-eight new sources, twenty-three new people records and three identity updates (Cronon, Worster and Loo confirmed on Wikidata by QLever), seven source-record URL and note corrections. Sol's review of 1.156 (findings 4, 6, 9, 10, 11, 14–18) applied; see release/fixes-1.156-C.md.

edge_386.evidence_note: Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md P.9 2) re-sourced this arrow from post to the new person entry ann_laura_stoler, keeping its id and kind, because its claim was hers alone. Earlier note retained: the checked publisher description of Race and the Education of Desire (1995) records a critique of the marginal place of empire, and of race in the making of bourgeois sexuality, in Foucault alongside productive use of his 1976 lectures and Dutch and French colonial archives; the book itself is unread; Spivak's critique of Foucault is the separate edge from her person entry. edge_417.relationship: Sexuality and racial formation investigated through colonial archives: 'the micromanagement of sexual arrangements … was critical to the distinctions between ruler and ruled' (1995, as quoted by Gouda); 'sexual control was both an instrumental image for the body politic … and itself fundamental to how racial policies were secured' (2002, p. 78, as quoted by Ottevaere)
edge_417.evidence_note: Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md P.9 2) re-sourced this arrow from post to the new person entry ann_laura_stoler, keeping its id and kind. Earlier note retained: the 1995 project both uses and questions Foucault; this contribution is the specific colonial-historical intervention described by the publisher, not the origin of queer history or proof that all queer historians adopted it. Added: Gouda 2009, p. 553 (read in full), quoting the 1995 book without a page; Ottevaere 2004 (read in full), quoting Carnal Knowledge, p. 78.

edge_892.relationship: Settler colonialism as 'a structure not an event': settler colonizers 'come to stay'; the form 'destroys to replace', is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal', has territory as its 'irreducible element' and persists after the frontier as 'structural genocide' (1994–2006)
edge_892.evidence_note: Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_01): the 2006 essay, read in full in the Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page (screq_wolfe_2006 addendum), joins the 1999 introduction (pp. 1–2, read earlier: settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies'; 'invasion is a structure not an event'; contents and catalogue checked). Wolfe 2006, in his words: 'Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal' (p. 387, pages per Kauanui 2016); 'Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event' (p. 388; his note 7 refers the formula to the 1999 book, p. 2, and to 'Nation and MiscegeNation', 1994, p. 96); 'Settler colonialism destroys to replace'; 'elimination refers to more than the summary liquidation of Indigenous people, though it includes that' (p. 390); 'settler colonialism is relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' (p. 403). A contribution, not a founding: earlier settler-society studies (1983, 1995) and earlier usage (Veracini 2013; Kauanui 2016, note 7: Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973) precede it, and Kauanui records that Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did'. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note (user rule, 2026-10-23); bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edge_893.relationship: A history of Victorian and Australian anthropology in its settler-colonial setting
edge_893.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1999). The contents page lists chapters on mother-right ('Sex and Property in Victorian Anthropology'), totemism ('Victorian Anthropology's Eternal Dichotomy') and E. B. Tylor ('Survival in a Paradigm Shift: E.B. Tylor and the Problem of the Text'), alongside virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse. Catalogue subjects: Anthropology -- Australia -- History; Racism in anthropology -- Australia. Introduction p. 1 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements'. The chapters' stance toward these anthropologists is not read here. If the introduction confirms a critical argument, a critique edge to anthropology/evolution may be the better reading. A historian's account of the discipline, not anthropological fieldwork. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_02): Veracini's obituary (read in full) reports that the 1999 book 'was ostensibly a history of Australian anthropology', that 'settler colonialism' was 'only added at the very end and at the request of the publisher', and that 'to explain the evolution of anthropology Patrick defined settler colonialism as distinct from colonialism'; Goeman (read in full) records Audra Simpson's memory of him as a historian 'of anthropology itself, and its relationship to politics'. The chapters remain unread, so the critique/contribution question stays open.

edge_882.relationship: Postcolonial studies 'failed to detect the settler colonial "situation" in its specific operation' (Veracini 2011); 'relying solely on postcolonial literatures … will not help to envision the shape that decolonization must take in settler colonial contexts' (Tuck and Yang 2012); postcolonial theory 'has tended to obscure the ongoing hierarchies of settler states' (Macoun and Strakosch 2013)
edge_882.evidence_note: Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_11): the arrow changes from an undirected comparison (post — settler_colonialism) to a directed critique from the field toward the umbrella (source settler_colonialism, target post; Sol review 1.156, finding 1), in three read texts' own words. Veracini 2011, p. 5 (read in full): 'colonial, imperial and postcolonial studies have primarily focused on something else … these scholarly literatures have ultimately failed to detect the settler colonial "situation" in its specific operation'; p. 1: 'colonial and settler colonial phenomena be analytically disentangled'. Tuck and Yang 2012, p. 5 (read): 'relying solely on postcolonial literatures or theories of coloniality that ignore settler colonialism will not help to envision the shape that decolonization must take in settler colonial contexts'. Macoun and Strakosch 2013 (author version, read), introduction: 'For many decades, postcolonial theory has shaped global scholarship of colonialism, and this has tended to obscure the ongoing hierarchies of settler states'; 'postcolonial does not "mean the same thing as post-settler colonial"'. Counter-reading kept: Hoxie 2008 (abstract) presents settler colonialism as the most promising aspect of a postcolonial critique. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note.

edge_881.relationship: Indigenous historical authority and settler-colonial analysis
edge_881.evidence_note: Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge settler colonial studies (abstract). Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_12) adds the read words on both sides. Kauanui 2016 (read in full): 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; Wolfe 'insisted … that Native scholars did' create the field; indigeneity 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'. Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014, pp. 9–11 (read): the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study'. Goeman 2016 (read in full): Wolfe's work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies that at times leaves out Indigenous epistemologies and ontologies'. Veracini 2013 (author manuscript, read): 'indigenous studies, and especially history became crucial disciplinary sites in the development of "settler colonialism" as a conceptual category'. Comparison only: Indigenous history is not a subset of the paradigm, and the paradigm did not originate there. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note.

edge_883.evidence_note: Veracini dates a usage, until the late 1970s, naming a diehard hyper-colonialism challenged by anti-colonial insurgencies. Mamdani revisits the first postcolonial generation's political economy (Rodney) to ask how settler and native became political identities. Comparison: no line of descent from liberation politics to the later field is asserted. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_13): Veracini 2011, pp. 5–7 (read in full), 'Decolonisation is not settler decolonisation': 'arguing against colonialism is not the same thing as condemning settler colonialism'; 'if colonialism ends with the coloniser's departure … settler colonialism ends with an indigenous ultimate permanence'. Tuck and Yang 2012, p. 31 (read): 'Decolonization is not equivocal to other anti-colonial struggles. It is incommensurable.' Both keep the two decolonisations apart, which is why a comparison and not a descent is drawn.

edge_112.relationship: Crosby and Melville connect introduced organisms with colonial expansion; Grove traces conservation through colonial networks; after 2000 McNeill's Something New Under the Sun (2000) and, with Engelke, The Great Acceleration (2016) write the twentieth century and the Anthropocene at world scale
edge_112.evidence_note: Ecological change and cross-border material relations provide one route beyond national containers; examples require attention to scale. Crosby’s temperate regions, Melville’s Mexican case and Grove’s island networks operate at different scales. Their books provide resources for histories across borders; this does not prove that all global historians adopted them. Subrahmanyam738n10 explicitly cites Crosby and Grove, adding named primary reception for this route; it does not establish every proposed Melville reception. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_112 revision): the Harvard University Press description of The Great Acceleration read ('The Earth has entered a new age—the Anthropocene'; 'human dependence on fossil fuels inaugurated the Anthropocene'); McNeill 2000 by metadata and prizes only.

edge_720.relationship: Environmental perspectives on city–hinterland connections, assessed in period by an urban historian as a contribution to urban history (1991–92); Castonguay and Evenden's Urban Rivers (2012) carry the city–river question across Europe and North America
edge_720.evidence_note: In-period evidence: the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis (open PDF, text layer read). The urban historian Timothy Mahoney judges that the book 'makes significant theoretical and substantive contributions to both economic and urban history by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context', and that Cronon 'has, perhaps inadvertently, brought urbanization as a “process” forward from its current relegation as a kind of assumed stage set for monographs on local occurrences in cities' (p. 491). Of the premise that 'to really understand how and why cities developed, one must study how they organized their hinterlands', he writes: 'Cronon’s study of Chicago demonstrates the explanatory power of this fundamental urban historical premise' (p. 492). He also finds that in the book 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491). Cronon’s response: 'One of my most important agendas in Nature’s Metropolis was to try to convince environmental historians that the city is among the most important historical loci of environmental change'; 'Surely such an argument can only strengthen the claims of urban history as a field, setting the process of urbanization in a broader context that is as important to urban historians as it is to environmental ones' (p. 520). The arrow rests on one book, one urban historian’s in-period assessment and the author’s reply; it does not claim that urban history as a field adopted environmental questions. Context only, not support for the claim: Cronon’s 1993 ASEH address names Joel Tarr’s 'many studies of pollution and waste streams' (p. 3, n. 6) and cites Melosi’s Garbage in the Cities (n. 24). cronon_urban_reception (2022) is a later reading. Cronon’s own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.131). Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_720 revision): the Pittsburgh page read (Mauch's blurb: 'the best environmental history of urban industrial rivers'); body unread.

edge_901.relationship: Ecological change as a two-way relation of people and nature, traced through property, markets and ideas of nature (1983–1995); and the field's institutions: ASEH president 1989–93, editor of the Weyerhaeuser Environmental Books 1994–2014 ('acquiring, editing, and writing forewords for all titles'), and in 2013 'the first self-described environmental historian ever to serve as president of the AHA'
edge_901.evidence_note: Cronon’s own in-period statements. Changes in the Land (1983), ch. 1 'The View from Walden', read in full in an unpaginated web transcription (page numbers not verified): 'The replacement of Indians by predominantly European populations in New England was as much an ecological as a cultural revolution'; 'An ecological history begins by assuming a dynamic and changing relationship between environment and culture, one as apt to produce contradictions as continuities. Moreover, it assumes that the interactions of the two are dialectical'; 'The choice is not between two landscapes, one with and one without a human influence; it is between two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'; 'The pig was not merely a pig but a creature bound among other things to the fence, the dandelion, and a very special definition of property'; a 'world capitalist system' draws people 'into trade and market relations which lie well beyond the boundaries of their local ecosystems'. He sets this against species-transfer accounts 'as Alfred Crosby and William H. McNeill have done', which are 'bound to be incomplete', and against functionalist ecological anthropology, which risks 'a static and ahistorical view'. In 1992 he calls Nature’s Metropolis 'a natural sequel' to that book, which 'described a comparable set of environmental changes that occurred in New England as that region became linked to London’s markets' (Annals of Iowa forum, p. 517). 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993): the lesson 'When people buy and sell things in a market, they link together ecosystems and encourage change' is 'a central concern of my own work' (p. 8, n. 14, citing Changes in the Land, Nature’s Metropolis and 'Kennecott Journey'); 'The chief moral of my own version of environmental history is the one I tried to embed in the title of my book Changes in the Land. To live as human beings on this planet is to change the world around us' (p. 19); 'the material history of environmental change is simultaneously a spiritual history of human consciousness and a political economic history of human society' (p. 19); 'All environmental knowledge is culturally constructed and historically contingent—including our own' (p. 14), held together with the claim that 'the natural world exists quite apart from what we believe about it' (p. 15). 'Kennecott Journey' (1992, p. 33): 'The special task of environmental historians is to tell stories that carry us back and forth across the boundary between people and nature to reveal just how culturally constructed that boundary is—and how dependent upon natural systems it remains.' 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995, author’s reflow p. 1): wilderness is 'quite profoundly a human creation'. A contribution, not a founding: he makes the claim for materialist analysis that tries 'to finesse a full-blown determinism' on behalf of the field ('One important contribution of environmental history', 1993, p. 13), and places the field among the 'new' histories of the 1960s (p. 2). Contested in period: Danbom (1992) reads Nature’s Metropolis for its 'environmental moralism' (p. 503) and as 'a book about evil unleavened by good' (p. 506); Cronon answers 'I see no pure heroes or pure villains in the stories I tell' (p. 522). His 1990 JAH response to Worster is unread. The 2003 afterword (pp. 182–185: property analysis learned from anthropology, economics and legal theory; his own criticism of schematic capitalism and source asymmetry) is a later reading. edge_342 (anthropology → environment) and edge_343 (environment → culture) stay: they record anthropology as a resource and environmental history’s contribution to cultural history; this arrow is his own framework. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_901 revision): CV pp. 2, 14–15 read in full; the AHA's open text of 'Storytelling' read in passages.
edge_901.map_label: Ecology, markets, ideas of nature and the field's institutions, 1983–2014

edge_903.relationship: Narrative bounded by evidence, ecology and the community of scholars: an environmental historian’s answer to postmodern critiques of narrative (1992); twenty years on, 'Storytelling' (2013) restated the case: 'How do we make the past come alive? By telling stories about it', referring readers to the 1992 essay for 'this theoretical background'
edge_903.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative', JAH 78:4 (March 1992), author-hosted copy in journal pagination (pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read). Writing about narrative, 'we cannot avoid encountering the postmodernist assault on narrative, which calls into question not just the stories we tell but the deeper purpose that motivated us in the first place' (p. 1349). The argument is meant for all historians: 'I am urging historians to acknowledge storytelling as the necessary core even of longue durée histories … Environmental history is but one example of these, and most of my arguments apply just as readily to the others' (p. 1349, n. 5). 'I, like most practicing historians, am only willing to follow the postmodernists so far'; 'My goal throughout has been to acknowledge the immense power of narrative while still defending the past (and nature) as real things to which our storytelling must somehow conform lest it cease being history altogether' (p. 1372). Three bounds: 'our stories cannot contravene known facts about the past' and 'our stories must make ecological sense' (p. 1372); 'We write as members of communities' (p. 1373). 'To just that extent, nature coauthors our stories' (p. 1373). Against 'an endless postmodernist deconstruction of texts that fails to ground itself in history, in community, in politics, and finally in the moral problem of living on earth' he asserts 'the virtues of narrative' (p. 1374), and he asks environmental historians for 'not just stories about nature, but stories about stories about nature' (p. 1375). He reads with Hayden White’s Metahistory, Tropics of Discourse and The Content of the Form and with Novick (nn. 6, 7, 43), and credits Richard White with the argument about criticism (n. 46). The 1993 address restates it: historical wisdom 'usually comes in the form of parables, not policy recommendations or certainties' (p. 16). This is his own text; no in-period reading that places the essay in the postmodernism debate was read. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_903 revision): the 2013 address read in passages (AHA open text; n. 14 refers to 'A Place for Stories').

edge_904.relationship: Three levels of environmental history (nature, modes of production, ideas), with the capitalist transformation of agriculture as the middle level (1979–1990); and, at the end, the 'Second Earth' of 1500 whose abundance gave 'the false impression that there was no limit' (Shrinking the Earth, 2016, as read by Collomb)
edge_904.evidence_note: Worster's own statements, in-period first. 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', The Ends of the Earth (1988), read in an abridged reprint and checked by full-text search of the 1988 edition, whose running heads place the passage between pp. 292 and 294 (Isenberg 2013 cites p. 293): 'There are three levels on which the new history proceeds, three clusters of issues it addresses'; 'The first deals with understanding nature itself, as organized and functioning in past times'; 'The second level in this history brings in the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment. Here we are concerned with tools and work, with the social relations that grow out of that work, with the various modes people have devised of producing goods from natural resources'; the third is 'the purely mental or intellectual, in which perceptions, ethics, laws, myths, and other structures of meaning become part of an individual's or group's dialogue with nature'; together they 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990; English text checked in Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature, ch. 4; JAH page as cited by Isenberg): 'most environmental historians seem to have settled philosophically on a position that is at once materialist and idealist', yet the essay turns to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena' (p. 1091), and proposes that 'the single most important task for scholars in the history of modern agroecology is to trace what Karl Polanyi has called “the great transformation”'. Dust Bowl (1979) had argued: 'Capitalism, it is my contention, has been the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature' (p. 5, as quoted by Cronon 1992, p. 1363; wording confirmed in the 1979 edition). In-period readings: Merchant's 1990 response (read) calls his 'conceptual levels of ecology (natural history), production (technology and its socioeconomic relations), and cognition' 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field', while the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' (p. 1117). Cronon (1992, read) finds that in Dust Bowl 'the chief agent of the story is not “the pioneers” or “civilization” or “man”; it is capitalism', a plot that 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy' (p. 1363). McDean (1986) criticises the generalisation across the Plains (existing source, not re-read). A contribution, not a founding: Worster takes the idea from Aldo Leopold, who 'spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history”' (1988), and McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013, pp. 88–89) reports White's and Cronon's 1990 objections ('superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense'; 'potentially excessive materialism'), whose texts are unread here; McNeill (2003, p. 37) writes of environmental historians' theories that 'The most cogent was probably the one elaborated in slightly different versions by both Donald Worster and Arthur McEvoy', but that such theories 'have sparked no groundswells of enthusiasm'. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_904 revision): Collomb 2017 para. 2 read in full; Shrinking the Earth itself unread; the Origins page (Hall chair from 1989 until retirement) and the AHA award list (2012) read.

text_revisions.old: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, acquired land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe's account of settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event treats invasion as a continuing relation rather than a completed frontier past. Lorenzo Veracini's work and the journal Settler Colonial Studies (2011) distinguished settler colonial from colonial phenomena. Comparative studies of settler capitalism and settler societies, and decolonization-era uses of the term, came earlier. In Canadian historical writing the framework meets an older historiography of dispossession, reserves, gender and the state in the West and British Columbia. It also meets Indigenous political theory of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence. Its uses extend to labour, science, memory and settler identity. The field is contested from several directions. Indigenous scholars ask whether it recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories. Historians question its structural inevitability and its fit across regions and periods, proposing other modes such as commercial penetration and extractivism. Black studies scholars question how it places slavery. Settler colonialism overlaps with Indigenous history, postcolonial critique and historical geography without being equivalent to any of them.
text_revisions.new: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, took land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe gave the field its programme: settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'invasion is a structure not an event' (1999, 2006). Lorenzo Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011) and distinguished colonialism ('you, work for me') from settler colonialism ('you, go away'), adding that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': it 'extinguishes itself'. Two questions organise this selection: how elimination persists while pursuing its own completion, and how settler-colonial analysis relates to Indigenous sovereignty, refusal and resurgence. Veracini develops Wolfe's formula: self-supersession means the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, not a successful decolonisation. The Indigenous reading adopts Wolfe's formula while insisting that 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies' (Kauanui), that 'decolonization is not a metaphor' (Tuck and Yang) and that refusal, not recognition, answers the settler state (Simpson, Coulthard). Settler scholars warn against 'colonial fatalism' (Macoun and Strakosch); Marxists ask whether elimination or exploitation defines the form (Englert). In Canada the frame met an older historiography of reserves, treaties, gender and the state, and the TRC's finding of 'cultural genocide' (2015).

text_revisions.old: Veracini disentangles settler colonial from colonial phenomena and introduces a dedicated journal (2011); a 2013 essay traces the concept's earlier career. Field-making, not a claim of single origin.
text_revisions.new: Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011; open access, volunteer-run, on an ARC grant; to Taylor & Francis in 2013) 'to contribute to the consolidation of a new scholarly field'. Colonialism says 'you, work for me'; settler colonialism says 'you, go away'; the two 'should be understood in their dialectical relation'. Developing Wolfe's formula rather than disputing it, he adds that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': 'settler colonialism, by contrast, extinguishes itself' and is 'least visible in the settler cities'. This self-supersession is the settler project's attempted extinction of the settler–Indigenous relation by the disappearance of Indigenous peoples, not a successful decolonisation, which would instead end 'with an indigenous ultimate permanence'; 'decolonisation is not settler decolonisation', and the politics of recognition 'cannot be considered a genuinely decolonising move' (2011). His history of the concept (2013) finds three earlier careers of the term and a consolidation 'from approximately the mid 1990s', with 'both the Canadian and US historiographies … late in adopting' it. Englert calls him Wolfe's 'self-styled intellectual successor'; Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel find in his history 'Indigenous studies and Indigenous resistance … pretty much erased'.

text_revisions.old: Reads the history of anthropology through settler colonialism. Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) studies virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse, and Victorian anthropology on mother-right, totemism and E. B. Tylor. Later essays address land, labour and race (2001) and the elimination of the native (2006).
text_revisions.new: An Australian historian of settler colonialism, race and the history of anthropology (1949–2016). His first book read Victorian and Australian anthropology through 'the elimination of native societies': 'the colonizers come to stay—invasion is a structure not an event' (1999). The 2006 essay made the formula a programme: settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; after the frontier, elimination 'turned inwards' through allotment, blood quantum and assimilation, so the form stays 'relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' names its convergence with genocide without 'hierarchy among victims'. Race, he argued, 'is made in the targeting' (2001, 2006; Traces of History, 2016). Veracini called him the field's founder 'in a fit of absentmindedness'; Kauanui records that he 'insisted … that he did not create the field … that Native scholars did'. Critics find in his structure a 'colonial fatalism' (Macoun and Strakosch) and ask whether exploitation, not elimination, defines settler colonies (Englert).

text_revisions.old: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model. Bullard’s environmental-justice inquiry and Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life histories broaden comparison toward unequal burdens, displacement and authority over historical accounts. Dust Bowl debates distinguish agricultural capitalism, technology and soils, federal intervention, regional scale and household survival; primary criticism and later social history complicate a single causal summary.

Bullard and the Huggins life histories add unequal burdens and authority over accounts; the Dust Bowl debates set capitalism, technology, policy and survival against one another. After 1995 the field argued with itself and its neighbours: Cronon called wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'; Foreman answered that this 'Received Wilderness Idea is a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground' (2000); Spence (1999) examined Indian removal in the making of national parks. A merged journal (1996), McNeill's world synthesis (2000) and a Canadian network (NiCHE, 2004) widened it; by 2013 Sutter found nature and culture replaced by 'environmental hybridity' (editors' summary). Chakrabarty (2009) and the Anthropocene histories of 2016 set its questions at planetary scale.

text_revisions.old: A historian of North American environments who treats ecological change as a two-way relation between people and the rest of nature, worked out through property, markets and ideas of nature. Changes in the Land (1983) assumes that 'the interactions of the two are dialectical' and finds in colonial New England not a choice between landscapes with and without people but 'two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'. Nature’s Metropolis (1991) follows grain, lumber and meat between Chicago and its hinterland on the premise that 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together'. 'A Place for Stories' (1992) asks environmental historians for 'stories about stories about nature', and 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) calls wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'. Reviewers found the Chicago book distant from farmers and townspeople, or moralising; he replied that he saw 'no pure heroes or pure villains'.

text_revisions.old: A historian of the American Great Plains and arid West who set out a three-level model of environmental history. In 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) he wrote that 'there are three levels on which the new history proceeds': 'understanding nature itself', 'the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment', and 'the purely mental or intellectual', which together 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. His 1990 Journal of American History essay turned to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', chiefly the capitalist transformation of agriculture, which Dust Bowl (1979) had called 'the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature'; Rivers of Empire (1985) described the West as 'a modern hydraulic society'. Merchant's 1990 response called the levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found that the essay 'lacks a gender analysis'. Cronon (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy'.
text_revisions.new: A historian of the American Great Plains and arid West who set out a three-level model of environmental history. In 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) he wrote that 'there are three levels on which the new history proceeds': 'understanding nature itself', 'the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment', and 'the purely mental or intellectual', which together 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. His 1990 Journal of American History essay turned to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', chiefly the capitalist transformation of agriculture, which Dust Bowl (1979) had called 'the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature'; Rivers of Empire (1985) described the West as 'a modern hydraulic society'. Merchant's 1990 response called the levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found that the essay 'lacks a gender analysis'. Cronon (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy'. After the round table he turned to lives and to limits: biographies of John Wesley Powell (2001) and John Muir (2008; the Muir essay of 2005), and Shrinking the Earth (2016), which Collomb read as a history of the 'Second Earth' of 1500 that gave settlers 'the false impression that there was no limit', by 'the greatest US environmental historian' — while finding its 'plea for an earth ethic almost rings hollow'. He held the Hall chair at Kansas from 1989 until retirement and received the AHA's Award for Scholarly Distinction (2012).

strand.title: Structure and its end: Wolfe and Veracini read together
strand.focus: Two emphases within one formula, not a documented exchange between opponents. Wolfe's structure is 'a continuity through time' that 'does not stop' with frontier homicide and 'has not been subject to election results' (2006). Veracini accepts the 'frequently quoted passage' and adds that 'the structure persistently pursues a specific end point' and 'extinguishes itself', so that settler colonialism 'covers its tracks' (2011): the end point is the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, which Veracini distinguishes from decolonisation. The History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) records the two authors co-cited by 3.0% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, a readership pairing that does not itself establish a dispute. Englert reads both as drawing 'a sharp analytical separation' between eliminatory settler and exploitative franchise colonies and finds the separation does not fit Africa or South America (2020); Macoun and Strakosch find in the structure a 'colonial fatalism' and recall the label 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world' (2013): these readings establish different emphases placed on the same structure. Veracini's obituary records Wolfe as 'still a Marxist' of 'the young Marx' for whom 'things are not things in themselves but relationships' (2016).
strand.works: Wolfe, "Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native" (2006); Veracini, "Introducing settler colonial studies" (2011) and "Patrick Wolfe (1949–2016)" (2016); Macoun and Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory" (2013); Englert, "Settlers, Workers, and the Logic of Accumulation by Dispossession" (2020).

strand.title: Canadian history beside and under the frame, 2009–2020
strand.focus: Works that Canadian PhDs read with Wolfe and Veracini, few of which adopt his vocabulary. Treaty history (Miller 2009, a distinctive riser among Canadian PhDs inside the Indigenous family in the 2026-10-23 release), racialisation and law in British Columbia's 'contact zone' (Mawani 2009), settler self-examination after residential schools (Regan 2010; Battell Lowman and Barker 2015: 'Canada and Settler Colonialism', 'It's Always All About the Land'), starvation policy (Daschuk 2013), Indigenous women's work 'in modern Native ways' (McCallum 2014), the TRC's finding that Canada's policy aimed 'to eliminate Aboriginal governments … and … cause Aboriginal peoples to cease to exist as distinct … entities' and 'can best be described as "cultural genocide"' (2015), imperial family and archive (Perry 2015), women homesteaders in 'the spadework of British colonialism' who 'took part in dispossessing Indigenous people' (Carter 2016), the settler-colonial city (Hugill 2017), the settler order in working-class history (Burrill 2019), Japanese Canadian dispossession (Stanger-Ross 2020), and Harris's reflections (2020). Veracini's own history says the Canadian historiography was 'late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis' (2013). Publisher descriptions, not the books, are read; none of Miller, Daschuk, McCallum, Perry 2015, Carter 2016 or Stanger-Ross uses the phrase on its page.

strand.title: A field's institutions: journal, associations, memorials
strand.focus: NAISA founded 2008 after an ASA panel of 2002 asked whether American Studies could be 'an intellectual home' for Native studies (Kauanui). Settler Colonial Studies founded 2011 'in an open access format (entirely run on volunteer labour)' and moved to Taylor & Francis 'within two years' (Snelgrove et al.; Edmonds and Carey 2013). Wolfe edited paired issues of the journal and of AICRJ (2013) and answered the binary charge with The Settler Complex (2016). ASA 2015: Goldstein's reappraisal and Warrior's count of panels. Wolfe's death (18 February 2016) brought obituaries from the journal (Veracini), AICRJ (Goeman), Aboriginal History (Birch) and an American Quarterly forum (2017); a Festschrift followed (Race, Place, Trace, 2022).
strand.works: Kauanui (2016); Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014); Edmonds and Carey, "A New Beginning for Settler Colonial Studies" (2013); Wolfe, ed., "Recuperating Binarism" (2013) and The Settler Complex (2016); Veracini (2016); Goeman (2016); Birch (2016); American Quarterly 69:2 (2017); Slyomovics and Veracini, eds., Race, Place, Trace (2022).

strand.title: The wilderness debate, 1995–2000: a selected exchange
strand.focus: Cronon's essay (1995; reprinted with comments in the first number of Environmental History, January 1996) held wilderness to be 'quite profoundly a human creation' and 'a flight from history' while defending wild-land protection. Hays replied in the journal that 'Cronon's wilderness is a world of abstracted ideas … divorced from the values and ideas inherent in wilderness action' (as quoted by Foreman; comment unread). Sessions objected from conservation biology (1996). Callicott and Nelson gathered thirty-nine essays as The Great New Wilderness Debate (1998), where Foreman's 'Wilderness Areas for Real' answered. Foreman then told a federal wilderness-science conference (1999; printed 2000) that he came 'not to praise The Received Wilderness Idea, but to bury it': the idea that 'Baird Callicott, Bill Cronon and other postmodern deconstructionist scholars so eagerly banish' was 'a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground', unlike 'the Real Wilderness Idea' that built the National Wilderness Preservation System. A selected exchange: Cohen's and Dunlap's comments, the editors' introduction to the anthology and Cronon's 1996 response (pp. 47–55) are unread; in 2003 he answered in practice, asking that the Apostle Islands be managed 'as a historical wilderness' — 'Emphatically yes' to designation, but 'a storied wilderness'.
strand.works: 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995; Environmental History 1:1, 1996, with comments and a response); Callicott and Nelson, eds., The Great New Wilderness Debate (1998); Foreman, 'The Real Wilderness Idea' (2000); Cronon, 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands' (2003)

strand.title: The Anthropocene and the climate of history
strand.focus: Chakrabarty's four theses (2009) held that anthropogenic climate change collapses the distinction between natural and human history (edge_918; critics at edge_1147). Environmental historians then wrote the epoch: McNeill and Engelke's The Great Acceleration (2016) says 'The Earth has entered a new age—the Anthropocene' and that 'human dependence on fossil fuels inaugurated' it; Malm's Fossil Capital (2016) answers that 'steam offered neither cheaper nor more abundant energy' but control over labour, against what a reviewer on its cover calls the 'Anthropocene narrative'; Bonneuil and Fressoz refuse 'the convenient view of a "human species" that upset the Earth system, unaware of what it was doing' (publisher descriptions; bodies unread). Worster's Shrinking the Earth (2016) was read by Collomb as 'reflections of the greatest US environmental historian on humankind's future and the Anthropocene'. McNeill told the AHA (2020) that 'environmental history stands to be disrupted, and with luck enhanced, more than most fields'. In PhD bibliographies this is a strand of the historiography, not of reading: Chakrabarty is cited by 4.5% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, in three families (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).
strand.works: Chakrabarty, 'The Climate of History' (2009); McNeill and Engelke, The Great Acceleration (2016); Malm, Fossil Capital (2016); Bonneuil and Fressoz, The Shock of the Anthropocene (2016); Worster, Shrinking the Earth (2016)

strand.title: Canadian environmental history: a network and a series, 2001–2019
strand.focus: Wynn (2003) found the field 'undeveloped in this country, compared with the United States'. Within a decade it had institutions: NiCHE, 'founded in fall 2004 by a small team of scholars' and funded by a SSHRC Strategic Knowledge Cluster grant from 2007 (MacEachern director; Wynn, Turkel, Castonguay, Evenden and Piper on the executive); Wynn's UBC Press series Nature | History | Society, 'devoted to the publication of high-quality scholarship in environmental history and allied fields'; and a Canadian number of Environmental History (October 2007, edited by Evenden and MacEachern) in which Piper and Sandlos found that 'the Canadian North was never subject to the broad ecological transformation that occurred further to the south' and Loo argued that environmental justice 'requires coming to terms with the different scales' at which change is apprehended. The books — MacEachern on Atlantic parks (2001), Evenden on the Fraser (2004), Loo on wildlife (2006), Sandlos on northern game laws (2007), Piper on subarctic industry (2009), Parr on the senses (2010), Colpitts on pemmican (2014), Loo on relocation (2019) — won the CHA's prizes and, in Canadian PhD bibliographies, entered the company of Cronon, Worster and White in 2010–19 (MacEachern and Loo in 2010–14; Parr, Piper, Evenden and Sandlos in 2015–19; History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23). Loo (2014) asked the field to 'use more of the world, and vice versa'.
strand.works: NiCHE (2004); Nature | History | Society (UBC Press); Environmental History 12:4 (2007); MacEachern (2001), Evenden (2004), Loo (2006, 2019), Sandlos (2007), Piper (2009), Parr (2010), Colpitts (2014); Loo, 'Missed Connections' (2014)

strand.title: Conservation, dispossession and neighbouring historiographies
strand.focus: Cronon wrote that 'The removal of Indians to create an "uninhabited wilderness"' showed 'just how invented, just how constructed, the American wilderness really is' (1995). Spence (1999) examined Indian removal in the making of national parks: Dispossessing the Wilderness traced how 'the early conception of the wilderness as the place where Indians lived (or should live)' gave way to 'the idealization of uninhabited wilderness' at Yellowstone, Glacier and Yosemite. Warren's The Hunter's Game (1997) and Jacoby's Crimes against Nature (2001; Marsh and Littleton-Griswold prizes), by Cronon's doctoral students, wrote the social history of poaching and conservation (unread; no reader read here links them to the wilderness essay). In Canada, Binnema and Niemi (2006) argued that the Stoney were excluded from Banff for game conservation, sport hunting, tourism and assimilation rather than for a wilderness ideal, and Sandlos (2007) that game laws and sanctuaries 'helped the state assert authority over traditional hunting cultures'; Daschuk's Clearing the Plains (2013), with disease and climate among its causes, is blurbed by McNeill and read with Wolfe. The dissertation record records an associated readership pattern: the works newly co-cited with the field's founders after 2015 are Wolfe, Tuck and Yang, The Middle Ground, Hämäläinen, DuVal and O'Brien (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23; founders Cronon ×3, Worster ×3, White, Crosby, Merchant; lift ≥ 3; averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses). Settler colonial studies is its own entry; the link between the two is drawn there.
